quiz.title: Unit 9 SAQ 01
quiz.headline: Nixon and the price of pollution
quiz.prompt: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question.
quiz.instructions: Answer all three parts. For each part, Answer the question directly, Prove it with specific historical evidence, and Explain how the evidence supports your answer. On the AP exam each part earns one point. This is self-assessment practice, not official College Board scoring.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP short-answer format. Model answers show one strong response; other accurate, well-supported answers can earn the point.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Richard Nixon, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 22, 1970
stimulusBlocks.citation: Richard Nixon, Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union, January 22, 1970. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/1970-Nixon.txt, converted to UTF-8).
stimulusBlocks.note: Three months later, millions of Americans took part in the first Earth Day, and in December 1970 the federal Environmental Protection Agency began work.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The great question of the seventies is, shall we surrender to our surroundings, or shall we make our peace with nature and begin to make reparations for the damage we have done to our air, to our land, and to our water? . . .

We still think of air as free. But clean air is not free, and neither is clean water. The price tag on pollution control is high. Through our years of past carelessness we incurred a debt to nature, and now that debt is being called. . . .

We can no longer afford to consider air and water common property, free to be abused by anyone without regard to the consequences. . . . This requires comprehensive new regulations. It also requires that, to the extent possible, the price of goods should be made to include the costs of producing and disposing of them without damage to the environment.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, or explain.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific person, place, institution, or development.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE claim Nixon makes about the cost of pollution.
criteria: States a specific claim from the passage.
Connects it to the cost of pollution or its control.

model.answer: Nixon claims that clean air and water have a real cost that the country can no longer ignore.
model.prove: He says that “clean air is not free, and neither is clean water,” and that past carelessness created “a debt to nature” that “is being called.”
model.explain: By describing pollution as a debt, he argues that Americans must now pay to repair damage they once treated as free.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify his claim that the price of goods should include the cost of producing and disposing of them without harming the environment.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way that economic or population growth in the period 1900 to the present contributed to the environmental problems Nixon describes.
criteria: Names a specific economic or demographic development.
Explains how it damaged air, land, or water.

model.answer: Industrial growth powered by fossil fuels released pollutants into the air and water.
model.prove: After World War II, factories, power plants, and tens of millions of new cars burned coal and oil, and Nixon himself called the automobile the country's worst air polluter.
model.explain: As production and consumption grew, so did emissions and waste, which damaged the air, land, and water Nixon wanted to restore.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain how rapid population growth increased demand for land, water, and energy, or how the Green Revolution's fertilizers and pesticides polluted soil and water.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE limitation of Nixon's speech as evidence for understanding global debates about the environment after 1970.
criteria: Identifies a specific feature of the source's purpose, audience, or perspective.
Explains why it limits what the source shows about global debates.

model.answer: The speech presents the view of a wealthy industrial country and focuses only on American air, land, and water.
model.prove: Nixon was addressing Congress to win support for US laws, and he speaks of clean air and water as the “birthright of every American.”
model.explain: It does not show the view of developing countries, which later argued at Kyoto that rich nations had caused most pollution and that poorer nations needed room to grow.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain that, as a political speech, it was meant to persuade and may promise more than the government later delivered, or that it predates scientific concern about global warming.
